\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Universality and its residual parameters}

A continuous phase transition is characterised by a divergent correlation
length and by power-law singularities in the thermodynamic observables. The
exponents of those power laws are \emph{universal}: they are insensitive to
almost all microscopic details, depending only on the spatial dimension $d$ and
on the symmetry of the order parameter. The liquid--vapour critical point of a
simple fluid and the Curie point of a uniaxial ferromagnet, physically
unrelated, share the same exponents.

The symmetry data is captured by an integer $N$, the number of components of
the order-parameter field, together with the group $O(N)$ acting on them. The
classical members of the family are

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}cll@{}}
\toprule
$N$ & Universality class & Physical realisation \\
\midrule
$0$ & Self-avoiding walk & Long polymer in solution \\
$1$ & Ising & Uniaxial magnet, simple fluid, binary alloy \\
$2$ & XY & Superfluid ${}^4$He, planar magnet \\
$3$ & Heisenberg & Isotropic ferromagnet \\
$\infty$ & Spherical & Exactly solvable limit \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Most treatments compute exponents at a fixed $N$. The purpose of this work is
to carry $N$ as a \emph{free real parameter} through the entire computation and
to prove statements that hold uniformly on the admissible range. This exposes
structure that no single value can reveal: extrema in $N$, sign changes in $N$,
exact limiting behaviour, and a precise account of which thermodynamic
identities the truncated exponents respect.

\subsection{The $\varepsilon$-expansion}

The technical device is Wilson's. In $d = 4$ the $\varphi^4$ interaction is
marginal and the exponents take mean-field values; in $d < 4$ it is relevant.
Setting $d = 4-\varepsilon$ and treating $\varepsilon$ as infinitesimal places
the non-trivial fixed point of the renormalisation-group flow at a coupling of
order $\varepsilon$, hence within reach of perturbation theory. All quantities
are then obtained as power series in $\varepsilon$, and one evaluates at
$\varepsilon = 1$ for three dimensions.

We do not re-derive the Feynman-diagram combinatorics. Instead we isolate its
output --- a small number of polynomial coefficients, now rational functions of
$N$ --- and study rigorously everything that follows from it.

\section{Setup and normalisation}

\begin{definition}[Admissible symmetry index]
A real number $N$ is \emph{admissible} if $N \ge 0$.
\end{definition}

Admissibility is what the physical family requires, and it is the hypothesis
under which all uniform bounds below are stated. Many results hold on the wider
formal range $N > -8$, and we state them there when they do. The only genuinely
excluded point is $N = -8$, where the one-loop quadratic coefficient vanishes
and the fixed point escapes to infinity.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:denom}
If $N$ is admissible then $N + 8 > 0$; in particular $N + 8 \neq 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from $N \ge 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[One-loop beta function]
For real $N, \varepsilon, g$,
\[
  \beta_N(\varepsilon, g) \;:=\; -\varepsilon\, g \;+\; \frac{N+8}{3}\, g^2 .
\]
\end{definition}

The normalisation is chosen so that at $N = 1$ the quadratic coefficient is
$3$, the standard one-component convention. The linear term is dimensional
analysis; the coefficient $N+8$ is the one-loop symmetry factor of the $O(N)$
vertex, decomposing as $N$ (an internal index loop) plus $8$ (the remaining
channel pairings with multiplicity).

\begin{definition}[Wilson--Fisher coupling]
\[
  g^{*}(N,\varepsilon) \;:=\; \frac{3\varepsilon}{N+8}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Coupling-dependent exponent functions]
\[
  \eta(N,g) := \frac{N+2}{18}\,g^{2},
  \qquad
  \frac{1}{\nu}(N,g) := 2 - \frac{N+2}{3}\,g .
\]
\end{definition}

These are the two-loop anomalous dimension and the one-loop inverse
correlation-length exponent as functions of the running coupling.

\begin{proposition}[Reduction to the one-component theory]
At $N = 1$: $\beta_1(\varepsilon,g) = -\varepsilon g + 3g^{2}$,
$g^{*}(1,\varepsilon) = \varepsilon/3$, and $\eta(1,g) = g^{2}/6$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Direct substitution.
\end{proof}

\section{Fixed points and stability}

\begin{theorem}[Classification of one-loop fixed points]\label{thm:classify}
Let $N \neq -8$ and let $\varepsilon, g$ be real. Then
\[
  \beta_N(\varepsilon, g) = 0
  \iff
  g = 0 \ \text{ or } \ g = g^{*}(N,\varepsilon).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Factor $\beta_N(\varepsilon,g) = g\bigl(-\varepsilon + \tfrac{N+8}{3}g\bigr)$.
A product of reals vanishes iff a factor does. The second factor vanishes iff
$\tfrac{N+8}{3}g = \varepsilon$, and since $N+8 \neq 0$ this is exactly
$g = 3\varepsilon/(N+8)$. Conversely both values are zeros by substitution.
\end{proof}

There is no third fixed point, formal or otherwise.

\begin{theorem}[Positivity and $N$-uniform bound]\label{thm:gstar-bound}
Let $N \ge 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Then
$0 < g^{*}(N,\varepsilon) \le 3\varepsilon/8$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Positivity is immediate. For the bound, compute the exact difference
\[
  \frac{3\varepsilon}{8} - g^{*}(N,\varepsilon)
  = \frac{3\varepsilon N}{8(N+8)} \ \ge\ 0 . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

The bound is attained at $N = 0$; the constant $3/8$ does not depend on $N$, so
the whole family is uniformly weakly coupled at criticality for small
$\varepsilon$.

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity in $N$]\label{thm:gstar-mono}
For $0 \le N_1 < N_2$ and $\varepsilon > 0$,
$g^{*}(N_2,\varepsilon) < g^{*}(N_1,\varepsilon)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$g^{*}(N_1,\varepsilon) - g^{*}(N_2,\varepsilon)
= 3\varepsilon(N_2-N_1)/\bigl((N_1+8)(N_2+8)\bigr) > 0$.
\end{proof}

More symmetry means a weaker fixed-point coupling, decaying like $3\varepsilon/N$.

\begin{lemma}[Differentiability]\label{lem:deriv}
For all $N, \varepsilon, g_0$, the map $g \mapsto \beta_N(\varepsilon,g)$ is
differentiable at $g_0$ with derivative $-\varepsilon + 2\tfrac{N+8}{3}g_0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Sum of the derivative of a linear map and of a constant multiple of
$g \mapsto g^{2}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Universality of $\omega$ at one loop]\label{thm:omega}
For every $N \neq -8$ and every $\varepsilon$,
\[
  \frac{\partial \beta_N}{\partial g}\Bigl|_{g = g^{*}(N,\varepsilon)}
  \;=\; \varepsilon .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Substitute into Lemma~\ref{lem:deriv}:
$-\varepsilon + 2\cdot\tfrac{N+8}{3}\cdot\tfrac{3\varepsilon}{N+8} = \varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

The slope at the infrared-stable fixed point is the correction-to-scaling
exponent $\omega$; hence $\omega = \varepsilon + O(\varepsilon^{2})$ for the
entire family at once, the $(N+8)$ of the beta-function coefficient cancelling
against the $(N+8)^{-1}$ of the fixed point.

\begin{theorem}[Exchange of stability]\label{thm:stability}
For $N \neq -8$ and $\varepsilon > 0$,
\[
  \frac{\partial\beta_N}{\partial g}\Bigl|_{g=0} = -\varepsilon < 0,
  \qquad
  \frac{\partial\beta_N}{\partial g}\Bigl|_{g=g^{*}} = \varepsilon > 0 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Lemma~\ref{lem:deriv} at $g_0 = 0$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:omega}.
\end{proof}

Under the infrared flow (direction $-\beta$) a positive slope means attraction.
Thus below four dimensions the Gaussian point is unstable, the Wilson--Fisher
point stable, and the crossover occurs at $\varepsilon = 0$ regardless of $N$.

\section{The critical exponents at first non-trivial order}

\begin{definition}\label{def:exponents}
For $N \neq -8$ set
\begin{align*}
  \eta(N,\varepsilon) &:= \frac{(N+2)\varepsilon^{2}}{2(N+8)^{2}}, &
  \nu(N,\varepsilon) &:= \frac12 + \frac{(N+2)\varepsilon}{4(N+8)}, &
  \gamma(N,\varepsilon) &:= 1 + \frac{(N+2)\varepsilon}{2(N+8)}, \\
  \alpha(N,\varepsilon) &:= \frac{(4-N)\varepsilon}{2(N+8)}, &
  \bop(N,\varepsilon) &:= \frac12 - \frac{3\varepsilon}{2(N+8)}, &
  \delta(\varepsilon) &:= 3+\varepsilon,
\end{align*}
and $\omega(\varepsilon) := \varepsilon$.
\end{definition}

We write $\bop$ for the order-parameter exponent to avoid collision with the
beta function. The exponents are, respectively: the anomalous dimension of the
critical two-point function; the correlation-length exponent; the
susceptibility exponent; the specific-heat exponent; the order-parameter
exponent; the critical-isotherm exponent; and the correction-to-scaling
exponent.

\begin{theorem}[Anomalous dimension at the fixed point]\label{thm:eta-at-fp}
For $N \neq -8$,
\[
  \eta\bigl(N, g^{*}(N,\varepsilon)\bigr)
  = \frac{N+2}{18}\Bigl(\frac{3\varepsilon}{N+8}\Bigr)^{2}
  = \frac{(N+2)\varepsilon^{2}}{2(N+8)^{2}}
  = \eta(N,\varepsilon).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\tfrac{N+2}{18}\cdot\tfrac{9\varepsilon^{2}}{(N+8)^{2}}
 = \tfrac{(N+2)\varepsilon^{2}}{2(N+8)^{2}}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Inverse correlation-length exponent]\label{thm:invnu}
For $N \neq -8$,
$\ \frac1\nu\bigl(N,g^{*}(N,\varepsilon)\bigr) = 2 - \frac{(N+2)\varepsilon}{N+8}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$2 - \tfrac{N+2}{3}\cdot\tfrac{3\varepsilon}{N+8}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Reciprocality defect]\label{thm:recip}
For $N \neq -8$,
\[
  \nu(N,\varepsilon)\cdot \frac1\nu\bigl(N,g^{*}(N,\varepsilon)\bigr)
  = 1 - \frac{(N+2)^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}{4(N+8)^{2}}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
With $u = (N+2)\varepsilon/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr)$ the product is
$(\tfrac12 + \tfrac u2)(2 - 2u) = 1 - u^{2}$.
\end{proof}

So $\nu$ and $1/\nu$ are reciprocal up to a defect of order $\varepsilon^{2}$,
precisely the order beyond which the one-loop truncation is not claimed valid.

\begin{proposition}[Specialisation at $N = 1$]\label{prop:N1}
At $N = 1$:
$\eta = \varepsilon^{2}/54$, $\nu = \tfrac12 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{12}$,
$\gamma = 1 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{6}$, $\alpha = \varepsilon/6$,
$\bop = \tfrac12 - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{6}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$N+2 = 3$, $N+8 = 9$, $4-N = 3$.
\end{proof}

At $\varepsilon = 1$ these give $\nu \approx 0.583$, $\gamma \approx 1.167$,
$\eta \approx 0.0185$, against the best three-dimensional Ising estimates
$\nu \approx 0.630$, $\gamma \approx 1.237$, $\eta \approx 0.036$: the correct
order of magnitude and the correct direction of deviation from mean field.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform physical admissibility]\label{thm:physical}
For every $N \ge 0$ and every $0 < \varepsilon \le 1$,
\[
  \eta > 0, \quad \nu > \tfrac12, \quad \gamma > 1, \quad
  0 < \bop < \tfrac12, \quad \alpha < 1, \quad \delta > 3 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\eta > 0$, $\nu > 1/2$, $\gamma > 1$ follow from positivity of $N+2$,
$\varepsilon$ and $N+8$. For $\bop$: $3\varepsilon/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr) > 0$
gives the upper bound, and $3\varepsilon \le 3 < N+8$ gives
$3\varepsilon/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr) < 1/2$, hence the lower bound. For $\alpha$:
if $N \le 4$ then $(4-N)\varepsilon \le 4 < 2(N+8)$; if $N > 4$ then
$\alpha \le 0 < 1$. Finally $\delta = 3+\varepsilon > 3$.
\end{proof}

\section{Uniform behaviour in the symmetry index}

Write the leading coefficients as functions of $N$ alone:
\[
  \eta_2(N) := \frac{N+2}{2(N+8)^{2}}, \quad
  \nu_1(N) := \frac{N+2}{4(N+8)}, \quad
  \alpha_1(N) := \frac{4-N}{2(N+8)}, \quad
  \gamma_1(N) := \frac{N+2}{2(N+8)},
\]
so $\eta = \eta_2(N)\varepsilon^{2}$, $\nu = \tfrac12 + \nu_1(N)\varepsilon$, and
so on. Note $\eta_2(1) = 1/54$ and $\nu_1(1) = 1/12$.

\begin{theorem}[Maximality at four components]\label{thm:eta-max}
For every real $N > -8$,
\[
  \eta_2(N) \le \frac{1}{48},
\]
with equality if and only if $N = 4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Since $N + 8 > 0$, the claim is equivalent to $48(N+2) \le 2(N+8)^{2}$, i.e.\
to $0 \le 2N^{2} - 16N + 32 = 2(N-4)^{2}$, true with equality iff $N = 4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[$N$-free bound on $\eta$]
For all $N \ge 0$ and all real $\varepsilon$,
$\ 0 < \eta_2(N)$ and
$\ \dfrac{(N+2)\varepsilon^{2}}{2(N+8)^{2}} \le \dfrac{\varepsilon^{2}}{48}$.
\end{corollary}

The mechanism is transparent:
$\tfrac{\dd}{\dd N}\tfrac{N+2}{(N+8)^{2}}$ has numerator
$(N+8)^{2} - 2(N+2)(N+8) = (N+8)(4-N)$.

\begin{theorem}[Two-sided monotonicity]\label{thm:eta-mono}
If $-8 < N_1 < N_2 \le 4$ then $\eta_2(N_1) < \eta_2(N_2)$. If
$4 \le N_1 < N_2$ then $\eta_2(N_2) < \eta_2(N_1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Cross-multiplying, the sign of $\eta_2(N_2) - \eta_2(N_1)$ is that of
\[
  2(N_2-N_1)\Bigl[6\bigl((N_1+8)+(N_2+8)\bigr) - (N_1+8)(N_2+8)\Bigr].
\]
With $x = N_1+8$, $y = N_2+8$, the bracket is $6(x+y) - xy$, positive when
$x < y \le 12$ and negative when $12 \le x < y$.
\end{proof}

Thus $\eta_2$ rises from $\eta_2(0) = 1/64$ through $1/54$, $1/50$, $5/242$ to
its maximum $\eta_2(4) = 1/48$, and then decreases to $0$.

\begin{theorem}[Strict monotonicity of $\nu_1$]\label{thm:nu-mono}
If $-8 < N_1 < N_2$ then $\nu_1(N_1) < \nu_1(N_2)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Reduces to $(N_1+2)(N_2+8) < (N_2+2)(N_1+8)$, i.e.\ $6N_1 < 6N_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform window for $\nu$]\label{thm:nu-window}
For every $N \ge 0$, $\ \tfrac{1}{16} \le \nu_1(N) < \tfrac14$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\nu_1(N) \ge 1/16 \iff 4(N+2) \ge N+8 \iff 3N \ge 0$, and
$\nu_1(N) < 1/4 \iff N+2 < N+8$.
\end{proof}

The lower endpoint is attained at $N = 0$; the upper endpoint $1/4$ is the
spherical-model value, approached but never attained at finite $N$.

\begin{theorem}[Antitonicity of $\alpha_1$]\label{thm:alpha-anti}
If $-8 < N_1 < N_2$ then $\alpha_1(N_2) < \alpha_1(N_1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Reduces to $(4-N_2)(N_1+8) < (4-N_1)(N_2+8)$, i.e.\ $-12N_2 < -12N_1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The specific heat stops diverging at four components]
\label{thm:alpha-sign}
For $N > -8$ and $\varepsilon > 0$,
\[
  \alpha > 0 \iff N < 4, \qquad
  \alpha = 0 \iff N = 4, \qquad
  \alpha < 0 \iff N > 4 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\alpha = (4-N)\varepsilon/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr)$ with $\varepsilon > 0$ and
$2(N+8) > 0$; the sign is that of $4-N$.
\end{proof}

For $N < 4$ the specific heat has a genuine power-law divergence; at $N = 4$
the leading exponent vanishes; for $N > 4$ it is finite with a cusp. It is
striking --- and traceable to the interplay of the factors $N+2$ and $N+8$ ---
that $N = 4$ is simultaneously the extremum of $\eta_2$ and the zero of
$\alpha_1$.

\begin{theorem}[Collapse to Gaussian at $N = -2$]\label{thm:gaussian}
$\eta_2(-2) = \nu_1(-2) = \gamma_1(-2) = 0$; consequently at $N = -2$ the
first-order exponents are the mean-field values $\eta = 0$, $\nu = 1/2$,
$\gamma = 1$. Moreover, if $N \neq -8$ and $\nu_1(N) = 0$, then $N = -2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Each of the three coefficients has $(N+2)$ as numerator; and
$\nu_1(N) = 0$ with non-vanishing denominator forces $N + 2 = 0$.
\end{proof}

\section{Large $N$ and the spherical-model cross-check}

\begin{lemma}[Partial fractions]\label{lem:partial}
For $N \neq -8$, with $t = (N+8)^{-1}$,
\[
  \eta_2(N) = \frac{t}{2} - 3t^{2}, \qquad
  \nu_1(N) = \frac14 - \frac32 t, \qquad
  \alpha_1(N) = -\frac12 + 6t .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$N+2 = (N+8) - 6$ and $4-N = 12 - (N+8)$; substitute and divide.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Large-$N$ limits]\label{thm:largeN}
As $N \to \infty$,
$\eta_2(N) \to 0$, $\nu_1(N) \to \tfrac14$, $\alpha_1(N) \to -\tfrac12$,
$\gamma_1(N) \to \tfrac12$; equivalently $\eta \to 0$,
$\nu \to \tfrac12 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{4}$, $\alpha \to -\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$,
$\gamma \to 1 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$t = (N+8)^{-1} \to 0$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:partial} and the algebra of limits.
\end{proof}

The $N \to \infty$ limit of the $O(N)$ model is the \emph{spherical model},
solvable in closed form for $2 < d < 4$, with
\[
  \nu_{\sph} = \frac{1}{d-2}, \qquad
  \alpha_{\sph} = \frac{d-4}{d-2}, \qquad
  \eta_{\sph} = 0 ,
\]
i.e.\ $1/(2-\varepsilon)$ and $-\varepsilon/(2-\varepsilon)$ in
$d = 4-\varepsilon$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact $\nu$-discrepancy and bound]\label{thm:sph-nu}
For $\varepsilon \neq 2$,
\[
  \frac{1}{2-\varepsilon} - \Bigl(\frac12 + \frac{\varepsilon}{4}\Bigr)
  = \frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{4(2-\varepsilon)} ,
\]
and for $|\varepsilon| \le 1$ the absolute value of this quantity is at most
$\varepsilon^{2}/4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Over the common denominator $4(2-\varepsilon)$ the numerator is
$4 - (2+\varepsilon)(2-\varepsilon) = \varepsilon^{2}$. For the bound,
$|\varepsilon| \le 1$ gives $2-\varepsilon \ge 1$, hence
$4(2-\varepsilon) \ge 4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact $\alpha$-discrepancy and bound]\label{thm:sph-alpha}
For $\varepsilon \neq 2$,
\[
  \frac{-\varepsilon}{2-\varepsilon} - \Bigl(-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\Bigr)
  = \frac{-\varepsilon^{2}}{2(2-\varepsilon)} ,
\]
and for $|\varepsilon| \le 1$ the absolute value is at most $\varepsilon^{2}/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Common denominator $2(2-\varepsilon)$; the numerator is
$-2\varepsilon + \varepsilon(2-\varepsilon) = -\varepsilon^{2}$.
\end{proof}

Together with $\eta_2 \to 0 = \eta_{\sph}$, this is a genuine consistency test:
a perturbative construction valid a priori only near $d = 4$ is confirmed at
the opposite extreme of the symmetry parameter by a non-perturbative exact
solution.

\section{Scaling relations and the linearity principle}

Classical scaling theory predicts
\[
  \alpha + 2\bop + \gamma = 2 \ \text{(Rushbrooke)}, \quad
  \gamma = \nu(2-\eta) \ \text{(Fisher)}, \quad
  2-\alpha = d\nu \ \text{(Josephson)}, \quad
  \delta = 1 + \gamma/\bop \ \text{(Widom)}.
\]
Truncated exponents need not satisfy these exactly; we determine which do.

\begin{theorem}[Rushbrooke is an identity]\label{thm:rush}
For every $N \neq -8$ and every $\varepsilon$,
$\ \alpha + 2\bop + \gamma = 2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The constant terms give $0 + 1 + 1 = 2$. The $\varepsilon$-terms have common
denominator $2(N+8)$ and numerator $(4-N) - 6 + (N+2) = 0$, identically in $N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$\gamma = 2\nu$ exactly]\label{thm:gamma2nu}
For every $N \neq -8$ and every $\varepsilon$, $\ \gamma = 2\nu$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$2\nu = 1 + (N+2)\varepsilon/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr) = \gamma$ term by term.
\end{proof}

Consequently the naive reading of Fisher's relation, $\eta = 2 - \gamma/\nu$,
returns $\eta = 0$, contradicting Theorem~\ref{thm:eta-at-fp}. The correct
exact statement is a deficit identity.

\begin{theorem}[Exact Fisher deficit]\label{thm:fisher}
For every $N \neq -8$,
$\ \gamma - \nu(2-\eta) = \nu\eta$, a quantity of order $\varepsilon^{2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:gamma2nu}, $\gamma - \nu(2-\eta) = 2\nu - 2\nu + \nu\eta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact Josephson deficit]\label{thm:josephson}
In $d = 4-\varepsilon$, for every $N \neq -8$,
\[
  (2-\alpha) - (4-\varepsilon)\nu = \frac{(N+2)\varepsilon^{2}}{4(N+8)} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Expand $(4-\varepsilon)\nu = 2 + \tfrac{(N+2)\varepsilon}{N+8}
- \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} - \tfrac{(N+2)\varepsilon^{2}}{4(N+8)}$. The
$\varepsilon^{1}$ terms of the difference have numerator over $2(N+8)$ equal to
$-(4-N) - 2(N+2) + (N+8) = 0$; the constants cancel; the stated
$\varepsilon^{2}$ term remains.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact Widom deficit]\label{thm:widom}
For $N \neq -8$ and $N + 8 - 3\varepsilon \neq 0$,
\[
  1 + \frac{\gamma}{\bop} - \delta
  = \frac{3\varepsilon^{2}}{N+8-3\varepsilon} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Over the denominator $2(N+8)$,
$\bop = \bigl(N+8-3\varepsilon\bigr)/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr)$ and
$\gamma = \bigl(2(N+8)+(N+2)\varepsilon\bigr)/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr)$, so
$\gamma/\bop = \bigl(2(N+8)+(N+2)\varepsilon\bigr)/D$ with
$D = N+8-3\varepsilon$. The numerator of
$1 + \gamma/\bop - (3+\varepsilon)$ over $D$ is
\[
  -(2+\varepsilon)D + 2(N+8) + (N+2)\varepsilon
  = 6\varepsilon + 3\varepsilon^{2} - (N+8)\varepsilon + (N+2)\varepsilon
  = 3\varepsilon^{2}. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

The $O(\varepsilon)$ part cancels for every $N$ simultaneously, and the
numerator of the leading defect is $N$-independent.

\begin{theorem}[Order-parameter deficit]\label{thm:beta-deficit}
For $N \neq -8$,
$\ \nu(2 - \varepsilon + \eta) - 2\bop
 = \nu\eta - \dfrac{(N+2)\varepsilon^{2}}{4(N+8)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The relation $2\bop = \nu(d-2+\eta)$ with $d = 4-\varepsilon$; the
$\varepsilon^{1}$ parts cancel, and the residue is the difference of the two
$O(\varepsilon^{2})$ deficits already computed.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Coupling--exponent identity]\label{thm:coupling-id}
For every $N \neq -8$ and every $\varepsilon$,
$\ 3\,\eta(N,\varepsilon) = \bigl(2\nu(N,\varepsilon) - 1\bigr)\,g^{*}(N,\varepsilon)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$2\nu - 1 = (N+2)\varepsilon/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr)$; multiplying by
$g^{*} = 3\varepsilon/(N+8)$ gives
$3(N+2)\varepsilon^{2}/\bigl(2(N+8)^{2}\bigr) = 3\eta$.
\end{proof}

Both sides are $O(\varepsilon^{2})$; the anomalous dimension is thus not
independent data but is determined by the enhancement of $\nu$ and the strength
of the fixed-point coupling.

\begin{theorem}[$N$-independent invariants]\label{thm:invariants}
For every $N \neq -8$ and every $\varepsilon$,
\[
  \gamma = 2\nu, \qquad \alpha + 2\bop + \gamma = 2, \qquad
  \alpha = 2 - 4\nu + \frac{\varepsilon}{2}, \qquad
  \delta = 3+\varepsilon, \qquad \omega = \varepsilon .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The first two are Theorems~\ref{thm:gamma2nu} and~\ref{thm:rush}. For the
third, $4\nu = 2 + (N+2)\varepsilon/(N+8)$, so $2 - 4\nu + \varepsilon/2$ has
$\varepsilon$-numerator over $2(N+8)$ equal to $-2(N+2) + (N+8) = 4-N$, which
is $\alpha$. The last two are definitional at this order.
\end{proof}

\begin{principle}[Linearity principle]
At first order in $\varepsilon$, the whole one-parameter family of $O(N)$
exponent vectors $(\alpha, \bop, \gamma, \delta, \nu, \eta, \omega)$ lies,
modulo the $O(\varepsilon^{2})$ entry $\eta$, on a single affine line in
exponent space, parameterised by $\nu$ alone. Consequently every scaling
relation \emph{affine} in the exponents holds identically in $(N,\varepsilon)$
--- this is why Rushbrooke is exact --- while every relation \emph{nonlinear}
in the exponents acquires a deficit equal to its second-order Taylor term along
that line --- this is why Fisher, Widom and Josephson each carry an explicitly
computable $O(\varepsilon^{2})$ defect.
\end{principle}

\section{The flow as a dynamical system}

The results so far concern fixed points and linearisations. It is a stronger,
genuinely dynamical statement that the Wilson--Fisher point attracts the flow
with a basin one can name. We prove this for the discrete (Euler) infrared
flow, which is what a numerical implementation actually iterates.

\begin{definition}[Discrete infrared flow]
Write $a_N := (N+8)/3$. Given $h > 0$ and $g_0$, set
\[
  g_{n+1} := g_n - h\bigl(-\varepsilon g_n + a_N g_n^{2}\bigr)
           = g_n\bigl(1 + h\varepsilon - h a_N g_n\bigr).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[One step preserves $(0,\varepsilon/a)$]\label{lem:step}
Let $a > 0$, $h > 0$ with $h\varepsilon \le 1$, and $0 < x < \varepsilon/a$.
Then $0 < x(1 + h\varepsilon - hax)$ and
$x\bigl(1 + ha(\varepsilon/a - x)\bigr) < \varepsilon/a$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Positivity: $ax < \varepsilon$ gives $1 + h\varepsilon - hax > 1$. For the
upper bound, the exact identity
\[
  \frac{\varepsilon}{a}
  - x\Bigl(1 + ha\bigl(\tfrac{\varepsilon}{a} - x\bigr)\Bigr)
  = \Bigl(\frac{\varepsilon}{a} - x\Bigr)\bigl(1 - hax\bigr)
\]
reduces the claim to positivity of the right side. The first factor is positive
by hypothesis; the second is non-negative since $hax < h\varepsilon \le 1$, and
cannot vanish, since $hax = 1$ with $ax < \varepsilon$ would force
$h\varepsilon > 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Invariance and monotonicity]\label{thm:flow-inv}
Let $N \ge 0$, $\varepsilon > 0$, $h > 0$ with $h\varepsilon \le 1$, and
$0 < g_0 < \varepsilon/a_N$. Then for every $n$,
$\ 0 < g_n < \varepsilon/a_N$ and $g_n < g_{n+1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $n$, using Lemma~\ref{lem:step} for invariance and
$g_{n+1} - g_n = h g_n(\varepsilon - a_N g_n) > 0$ for strict increase.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Wilson--Fisher is the infrared attractor]\label{thm:flow-conv}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:flow-inv},
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty} g_n = \frac{\varepsilon}{a_N} = \frac{3\varepsilon}{N+8}
  = g^{*}(N,\varepsilon).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The sequence is increasing and bounded above by $\varepsilon/a_N$, hence
converges to its supremum $L$. Passing to the limit in
$g_{n+1} = g_n(1 + h\varepsilon - h a_N g_n)$ gives
$L\,h(\varepsilon - a_N L) = 0$; since $L \ge g_0 > 0$ and $h > 0$, we get
$L = \varepsilon/a_N$.
\end{proof}

The basin $(0, g^{*})$ and the admissible step range $0 < h \le 1/\varepsilon$
are the same for every $N \ge 0$: the dynamical picture is $N$-uniform.

\section{Two loops: existence and $N$-uniform asymptotics}

At the next order the beta function is a genuine cubic,
\[
  \beta_N(\varepsilon,g) = -\varepsilon g + a g^{2} - c g^{3},
  \qquad a = \frac{N+8}{3},
\]
and its non-Gaussian zero is no longer a polynomial in $\varepsilon$. Rather
than manipulate formal power series, we work with the exact root and bound it.
Throughout, $c > 0$ is a free parameter, so the results are
scheme-independent; the standard choice in our normalisation is
$c = (3N+14)/9$.

\begin{theorem}[Existence of a small positive root]\label{thm:root-exists}
Let $a, c, \varepsilon > 0$ with $4c\varepsilon \le a^{2}$. Then there exists
$r \in [\varepsilon/a,\, 2\varepsilon/a]$ with $c r^{2} - a r + \varepsilon = 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Set $f(x) = cx^{2} - ax + \varepsilon$. Then $f(\varepsilon/a)
= c\varepsilon^{2}/a^{2} \ge 0$ and
$f(2\varepsilon/a) = (4c\varepsilon - a^{2})\varepsilon/a^{2} \le 0$. The
intermediate value theorem on $[\varepsilon/a, 2\varepsilon/a]$ supplies the
root.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Exact slope along the zero locus]\label{lem:slope}
If $c r^{2} - a r + \varepsilon = 0$ then
$\ -\varepsilon + 2ar - 3cr^{2} = \varepsilon - c r^{2}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$2(cr^{2} - ar + \varepsilon) = 0$ gives $2ar = 2cr^{2} + 2\varepsilon$;
substitute.
\end{proof}

The left side is $\partial_g\beta_N$ at $g = r$; the identity is algebraic, not
approximate. Setting $c = 0$ recovers Theorem~\ref{thm:omega}.

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative expansion of the fixed point]\label{thm:root-exp}
Let $a, c, \varepsilon > 0$ and let $r \in [\varepsilon/a, 2\varepsilon/a]$
satisfy $cr^{2} - ar + \varepsilon = 0$. Then
\[
  0 \;\le\; r - \Bigl(\frac{\varepsilon}{a} + \frac{c\varepsilon^{2}}{a^{3}}\Bigr)
    \;\le\; \frac{12\,c^{2}\varepsilon^{3}}{a^{5}} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The key identity, obtained by clearing $a^{3}$ and using the root equation, is
\[
  a^{3}\Bigl(r - \frac{\varepsilon}{a} - \frac{c\varepsilon^{2}}{a^{3}}\Bigr)
  = c\,(ar - \varepsilon)(ar + \varepsilon).
\]
Both factors are non-negative since $ar \ge \varepsilon$, giving the lower
bound. For the upper bound, the root equation gives $ar - \varepsilon = cr^{2}$
and $r \le 2\varepsilon/a$ gives $r^{2} \le 4\varepsilon^{2}/a^{2}$, hence
$ar - \varepsilon \le 4c\varepsilon^{2}/a^{2}$; also
$ar + \varepsilon \le 3\varepsilon$. Multiplying and dividing by $a^{3}$
finishes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative expansion of $\omega$]\label{thm:omega-exp}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:root-exp},
\[
  \Bigl|\bigl(-\varepsilon + 2ar - 3cr^{2}\bigr)
        - \Bigl(\varepsilon - \frac{c\varepsilon^{2}}{a^{2}}\Bigr)\Bigr|
  \;\le\; \frac{12\,c^{2}\varepsilon^{3}}{a^{4}} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:slope} the quantity is $c\,(r^{2} - \varepsilon^{2}/a^{2})$
in absolute value. This bracket is non-negative since $r \ge \varepsilon/a$;
writing $r^{2} - \varepsilon^{2}/a^{2} = (ar-\varepsilon)(ar+\varepsilon)/a^{2}$
and reusing the bounds of the previous proof gives
$r^{2} - \varepsilon^{2}/a^{2} \le 12c\varepsilon^{3}/a^{4}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
The predicted two-loop fixed point of the $O(N)$ family is
\[
  g^{*}_{2}(N,c,\varepsilon)
  := \frac{3\varepsilon}{N+8} + \frac{27\,c\,\varepsilon^{2}}{(N+8)^{3}},
\]
which equals $\varepsilon/a + c\varepsilon^{2}/a^{3}$ with $a = (N+8)/3$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:cubic}
If $c g^{2} - \tfrac{N+8}{3}g + \varepsilon = 0$ then
$-\varepsilon g + \tfrac{N+8}{3}g^{2} - cg^{3} = 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The cubic equals $-g\bigl(cg^{2} - \tfrac{N+8}{3}g + \varepsilon\bigr)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$N$-uniform two-loop fixed point]\label{thm:twoloop}
Let $N \ge 0$ and $0 < \varepsilon \le 4/7$, and take $c = (3N+14)/9$. Then
there exists $g$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $-\varepsilon g + \tfrac{N+8}{3}g^{2} - cg^{3} = 0$;
\item $g \ge 3\varepsilon/(N+8)$;
\item $\bigl|g - g^{*}_{2}(N,c,\varepsilon)\bigr| \le \varepsilon^{3}$, the
constant $1$ being independent of $N$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Put $a = (N+8)/3 \ge 8/3$ and $c = (3N+14)/9 > 0$. The hypothesis
$4c\varepsilon \le a^{2}$ holds since $\varepsilon \le 4/7$ and
$4\cdot\tfrac{3N+14}{9}\cdot\tfrac47 \le \bigl(\tfrac{N+8}{3}\bigr)^{2}$ for
$N \ge 0$. Theorem~\ref{thm:root-exists} supplies $r \in [\varepsilon/a,
2\varepsilon/a]$; Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic} makes it a zero of the cubic; $r \ge
\varepsilon/a = 3\varepsilon/(N+8)$ gives (2); and Theorem~\ref{thm:root-exp}
gives $|r - g^{*}_{2}| \le 12c^{2}\varepsilon^{3}/a^{5}$. Finally $12c^{2}/a^{5}
\le 1$: since $c = \tfrac{3N+14}{9} \le \tfrac{N+8}{3} = a$, it suffices that
$12a^{2} \le a^{5}$, i.e.\ $a^{3} \ge 12$, which holds as $a \ge 8/3$ and
$(8/3)^{3} = 512/27 > 12$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two loops push the coupling up]\label{thm:push-up}
For $N \ge 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$,
$\ 3\varepsilon/(N+8) < g^{*}_{2}\bigl(N, (3N+14)/9, \varepsilon\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The difference is $27c\varepsilon^{2}/(N+8)^{3} > 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why uniformity is not automatic]
The remainder constant $12c^{2}/a^{5}$ contains $c^{2}$, which grows like
$N^{2}$. Uniformity depends essentially on $a = (N+8)/3$ appearing to the fifth
power, giving net behaviour $O(N^{-3})$. Physically: the two-loop remainder is
uniformly small \emph{because} the fixed-point coupling shrinks like $1/N$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:gstar-mono}). Highly symmetric models are weakly coupled at
criticality, consistent with the exact solvability of the $N = \infty$ limit.
\end{remark}

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What parameterisation buys}

Every individual formula in Definition~\ref{def:exponents} is classical. What
is new is the systematic treatment of $N$ as a variable and the resulting
global statements: an extremum theorem invisible at any single $N$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:eta-max}); sign-change and monotonicity statements
(Theorems~\ref{thm:eta-mono}--\ref{thm:alpha-sign}) with the same value $N = 4$
appearing twice for algebraically distinct reasons; exact deficits for every
scaling relation rather than the usual claim that they hold ``to this order'';
the linearity principle explaining the entire deficit table structurally; and
$N$-uniform dynamical and two-loop statements with explicit constants and
explicit ranges of validity.

\subsection{A cautionary case}

Two natural-sounding claims are false and had to be reformulated. First,
``Fisher's relation $\eta = 2 - \gamma/\nu$ holds to this order'' is false for
the truncated exponents: since $\gamma = 2\nu$ identically
(Theorem~\ref{thm:gamma2nu}), the right side is identically $0$, contradicting
$\eta > 0$. The correct statement is the deficit identity
$\gamma - \nu(2-\eta) = \nu\eta$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:fisher}). The lesson is
precisely the linearity principle: the truncation lies on the line
$\gamma = 2\nu$, so relations sensitive to the curvature of the exponent
manifold cannot be tested at this order. Second, ``the leading coefficients are
monotone in $N$'' is false for $\eta_2$: monotonicity holds only up to $N = 4$.
That apparent obstruction became the extremum theorem.

\subsection{Limitations}

The expansion is asymptotic, not convergent, and is evaluated at
$\varepsilon = 1$ for three dimensions, so first-order numerical accuracy is
modest. The exponents of Definition~\ref{def:exponents} are truncations and are
not claimed to satisfy any relation beyond the stated order; the deficits of
Section~7 quantify exactly this. The two-loop analysis treats $c$ as a positive
parameter and controls the exact root of the cubic, but does not derive $c$
diagrammatically. The $N \to \infty$ comparison is a first-order comparison with
explicit second-order error, not a proof that the expansion resums to the
spherical model.

\subsection{Numerical summary at $\varepsilon = 1$}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$N$ & $g^{*}$ & $\eta$ & $\nu$ & $\gamma$ & $\alpha$ & $\bop$ \\
\midrule
$0$      & $0.3750$ & $0.01563$ & $0.5625$ & $1.1250$ & $ 0.2500$ & $0.3125$ \\
$1$      & $0.3333$ & $0.01852$ & $0.5833$ & $1.1667$ & $ 0.1667$ & $0.3333$ \\
$2$      & $0.3000$ & $0.02000$ & $0.6000$ & $1.2000$ & $ 0.1000$ & $0.3500$ \\
$3$      & $0.2727$ & $0.02066$ & $0.6136$ & $1.2273$ & $ 0.0455$ & $0.3636$ \\
$4$      & $0.2500$ & $0.02083$ & $0.6250$ & $1.2500$ & $ 0.0000$ & $0.3750$ \\
$10$     & $0.1667$ & $0.01852$ & $0.6667$ & $1.3333$ & $-0.1667$ & $0.4167$ \\
$\infty$ & $0$      & $0$       & $0.7500$ & $1.5000$ & $-0.5000$ & $0.5000$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The $\eta$ column peaks at $N = 4$ and the $\alpha$ column changes sign there,
exactly as Theorems~\ref{thm:eta-max} and~\ref{thm:alpha-sign} predict. Every
row satisfies $\alpha + 2\bop + \gamma = 2$ and $\gamma = 2\nu$ exactly.

\subsection{Future directions}

\emph{A linear-relations-are-exact theorem.} The linearity principle should be
formulated and proved as a genuine theorem: characterise the affine subspace
containing the first-order exponent vector, and show that a polynomial relation
among exponents holds identically on the truncation if and only if it vanishes
on that subspace, with deficit equal to the leading nonvanishing Taylor term
along it. This would replace the case-by-case computations of Section~7 with a
single structural argument.

\emph{Higher orders with the same uniformity.} Extending Section~9 to the
quartic beta function requires either a root estimate one degree higher or a
contraction-mapping argument for the implicit function defining
$g^{*}(\varepsilon)$; the payoff would be $N$-uniform three-loop exponents with
explicit constants.

\emph{The full continuation in $N$.} Our uniform results are stated on
$N \ge 0$, several extending to $N > -8$. The behaviour on $(-8,-2)$ and near
$N = -8$, where the fixed point escapes to infinity, is well defined in the
truncated model and deserves its own analysis.

\emph{Resummation and $\varepsilon = 1$.} All bounds here concern the
truncation error of the series in $\varepsilon$, not the distance to the true
three-dimensional exponents. Combining the $N$-uniform structure found here
with Borel-type resummation is the natural route to uniform-in-$N$ error
control at $\varepsilon = 1$.

\emph{Anisotropic and constrained generalisations.} Replacing $O(N)$ by a
general symmetry group replaces the scalar $(N+8)/3$ by a matrix of couplings,
and the fixed-point classification becomes a system of quadratics. The analogue
of Theorem~\ref{thm:classify} --- a complete classification with a uniform
bound on the couplings --- is the natural next target.

\appendix

\section{Table of the leading coefficients}

With $t = (N+8)^{-1}$:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
Quantity & Rational form & Partial fractions & $N \to \infty$ \\
\midrule
$g^{*}/\varepsilon$ & $3/(N+8)$ & $3t$ & $0$ \\
$\eta/\varepsilon^{2}$ & $(N+2)/\bigl(2(N+8)^{2}\bigr)$ & $t/2 - 3t^{2}$ & $0$ \\
$(\nu - \tfrac12)/\varepsilon$ & $(N+2)/\bigl(4(N+8)\bigr)$ & $\tfrac14 - \tfrac32 t$ & $\tfrac14$ \\
$(\gamma - 1)/\varepsilon$ & $(N+2)/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr)$ & $\tfrac12 - 3t$ & $\tfrac12$ \\
$\alpha/\varepsilon$ & $(4-N)/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr)$ & $-\tfrac12 + 6t$ & $-\tfrac12$ \\
$(\tfrac12 - \bop)/\varepsilon$ & $3/\bigl(2(N+8)\bigr)$ & $\tfrac32 t$ & $0$ \\
$\delta - 3$ & $\varepsilon$ & --- & $\varepsilon$ \\
$\omega$ & $\varepsilon$ & --- & $\varepsilon$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Numerical demonstrations for the critical exponents of the O(N) model,
uniformly in the symmetry index N.

Everything in this file is derived from a single one-loop beta function

    beta_N(eps, g) = -eps * g + ((N + 8) / 3) * g**2,

whose only zeros are the Gaussian coupling g = 0 and the Wilson-Fisher
coupling g* = 3*eps/(N + 8).  Substituting g* into the standard scaling
functions produces the first terms of the critical exponents as explicit
rational functions of N:

    eta   = (N+2) eps^2 / (2 (N+8)^2)
    nu    = 1/2 + (N+2) eps / (4 (N+8))
    gamma = 1 + (N+2) eps / (2 (N+8))
    alpha = (4-N) eps / (2 (N+8))
    beta  = 1/2 - 3 eps / (2 (N+8))
    delta = 3 + eps
    omega = eps

The script verifies, numerically and to machine precision:

  1. the fixed-point classification and the value of g*;
  2. reduction to the classical one-component (Ising) values at N = 1;
  3. omega = d(beta_N)/dg at g*, equal to eps for every N;
  4. maximality of the eta coefficient exactly at N = 4, value 1/48;
  5. the sign flip of the specific-heat exponent exactly at N = 4;
  6. Rushbrooke's relation as an exact identity in (N, eps);
  7. the closed-form deficits of Fisher, Josephson and Widom;
  8. the coupling-exponent identity 3 eta = (2 nu - 1) g*;
  9. large-N limits and agreement with the exactly solvable spherical model;
 10. convergence of the discrete infrared flow to g*, N-uniformly;
 11. two-loop existence with an N-independent O(eps^3) remainder constant.

Requires only the Python standard library.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

TOL: float = 1e-12


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The one-loop flow
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def beta_one_loop(n_sym: float, eps: float, g: float) -> float:
    """One-loop beta function -eps*g + ((N+8)/3) g^2."""
    return -eps * g + ((n_sym + 8.0) / 3.0) * g * g


def beta_derivative(n_sym: float, eps: float, g: float) -> float:
    """Exact derivative d(beta)/dg = -eps + 2 ((N+8)/3) g."""
    return -eps + 2.0 * ((n_sym + 8.0) / 3.0) * g


def fixed_point(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Wilson-Fisher coupling g* = 3 eps / (N + 8)."""
    return 3.0 * eps / (n_sym + 8.0)


def beta_two_loop(n_sym: float, c_two: float, eps: float, g: float) -> float:
    """Two-loop beta function -eps*g + ((N+8)/3) g^2 - c g^3."""
    return beta_one_loop(n_sym, eps, g) - c_two * g ** 3


def two_loop_coeff(n_sym: float) -> float:
    """Standard two-loop coefficient c(N) = (3N + 14)/9 in this normalisation."""
    return (3.0 * n_sym + 14.0) / 9.0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The critical exponents
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def eta_exponent(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Anomalous dimension eta = (N+2) eps^2 / (2 (N+8)^2)."""
    return (n_sym + 2.0) * eps ** 2 / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0) ** 2)


def nu_exponent(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Correlation-length exponent nu = 1/2 + (N+2) eps / (4 (N+8))."""
    return 0.5 + (n_sym + 2.0) * eps / (4.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


def inv_nu_at_fixed_point(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """1/nu evaluated at the fixed point: 2 - (N+2) eps / (N+8)."""
    return 2.0 - (n_sym + 2.0) * eps / (n_sym + 8.0)


def gamma_exponent(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Susceptibility exponent gamma = 1 + (N+2) eps / (2 (N+8))."""
    return 1.0 + (n_sym + 2.0) * eps / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


def alpha_exponent(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Specific-heat exponent alpha = (4-N) eps / (2 (N+8))."""
    return (4.0 - n_sym) * eps / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


def beta_op_exponent(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Order-parameter exponent beta = 1/2 - 3 eps / (2 (N+8))."""
    return 0.5 - 3.0 * eps / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


def delta_exponent(eps: float) -> float:
    """Critical-isotherm exponent delta = 3 + eps (independent of N)."""
    return 3.0 + eps


def omega_exponent(eps: float) -> float:
    """Correction-to-scaling exponent omega = eps (independent of N)."""
    return eps


def all_exponents(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """Return the full exponent dictionary at given (N, eps)."""
    return {
        "g*": fixed_point(n_sym, eps),
        "eta": eta_exponent(n_sym, eps),
        "nu": nu_exponent(n_sym, eps),
        "gamma": gamma_exponent(n_sym, eps),
        "alpha": alpha_exponent(n_sym, eps),
        "beta": beta_op_exponent(n_sym, eps),
        "delta": delta_exponent(eps),
        "omega": omega_exponent(eps),
    }


# Leading coefficients as functions of N alone.


def eta_coeff(n_sym: float) -> float:
    """eta_2(N) = (N+2) / (2 (N+8)^2), the coefficient of eps^2 in eta."""
    return (n_sym + 2.0) / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0) ** 2)


def nu_coeff(n_sym: float) -> float:
    """nu_1(N) = (N+2) / (4 (N+8)), the coefficient of eps in nu."""
    return (n_sym + 2.0) / (4.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


def alpha_coeff(n_sym: float) -> float:
    """alpha_1(N) = (4-N) / (2 (N+8)), the coefficient of eps in alpha."""
    return (4.0 - n_sym) / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Reporting helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def check(label: str, lhs: float, rhs: float, tol: float = TOL) -> bool:
    """Print and return the outcome of a numerical equality assertion."""
    ok = abs(lhs - rhs) <= tol * max(1.0, abs(lhs), abs(rhs))
    mark = "OK " if ok else "FAIL"
    print(f"  [{mark}] {label:<52s} {lhs: .12f}  vs {rhs: .12f}")
    return ok


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 1: fixed-point classification and reduction at N = 1
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_fixed_points() -> None:
    banner("1.  Fixed points of the one-loop flow, and the Ising slice")
    eps = 1.0
    print("  beta_N(eps, g) = -eps g + ((N+8)/3) g^2 ;  eps = 1")
    print()
    print(f"  {'N':>6s} {'g*':>12s} {'beta(g*)':>14s} {'beta(0)':>10s}"
          f" {'slope at 0':>12s} {'slope at g*':>12s}")
    for n_sym in (0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 10.0, 100.0):
        g_star = fixed_point(n_sym, eps)
        print(f"  {n_sym:6.0f} {g_star:12.8f} {beta_one_loop(n_sym, eps, g_star):14.2e}"
              f" {beta_one_loop(n_sym, eps, 0.0):10.2e}"
              f" {beta_derivative(n_sym, eps, 0.0):12.6f}"
              f" {beta_derivative(n_sym, eps, g_star):12.6f}")
    print()
    print("  The Gaussian point has slope -eps < 0 (infrared-repulsive);")
    print("  the Wilson-Fisher point has slope exactly +eps > 0 for EVERY N.")
    print()
    print("  Reduction to the one-component (Ising) theory at N = 1, eps = 1:")
    check("g*(1, 1) = 1/3", fixed_point(1.0, 1.0), 1.0 / 3.0)
    check("eta(1, 1) = 1/54", eta_exponent(1.0, 1.0), 1.0 / 54.0)
    check("nu(1, 1) = 1/2 + 1/12", nu_exponent(1.0, 1.0), 0.5 + 1.0 / 12.0)
    check("gamma(1, 1) = 1 + 1/6", gamma_exponent(1.0, 1.0), 1.0 + 1.0 / 6.0)
    check("alpha(1, 1) = 1/6", alpha_exponent(1.0, 1.0), 1.0 / 6.0)
    check("beta(1, 1) = 1/2 - 1/6", beta_op_exponent(1.0, 1.0), 0.5 - 1.0 / 6.0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 2: omega is the slope, universally
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def numerical_derivative(f: Callable[[float], float], x: float,
                         h: float = 1e-6) -> float:
    """Central finite difference."""
    return (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2.0 * h)


def demo_omega_universality() -> None:
    banner("2.  omega = d(beta)/dg at the fixed point equals eps for every N")
    for eps in (0.25, 0.5, 1.0):
        print(f"  eps = {eps}")
        for n_sym in (0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 7.0, 50.0):
            g_star = fixed_point(n_sym, eps)
            num = numerical_derivative(lambda g: beta_one_loop(n_sym, eps, g), g_star)
            check(f"N = {n_sym:<5g}  finite-difference slope = eps",
                  num, omega_exponent(eps), tol=1e-6)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 3: the extremum at N = 4
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_extremum_at_four() -> None:
    banner("3.  The anomalous-dimension coefficient peaks exactly at N = 4")
    print("  eta_2(N) = (N+2) / (2 (N+8)^2);   claim: max = 1/48 at N = 4")
    print()
    print(f"  {'N':>8s} {'eta_2(N)':>14s} {'1/48 - eta_2':>16s} "
          f"{'alpha_1(N)':>12s}")
    grid: List[float] = [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0, 8.0, 20.0, 200.0]
    for n_sym in grid:
        print(f"  {n_sym:8.2f} {eta_coeff(n_sym):14.10f} "
              f"{1.0 / 48.0 - eta_coeff(n_sym):16.3e} {alpha_coeff(n_sym):12.6f}")
    print()
    # Fine scan to locate the maximiser numerically.
    best_n, best_v = -8.0, -math.inf
    n_val = 0.0
    while n_val <= 12.0:
        v = eta_coeff(n_val)
        if v > best_v:
            best_n, best_v = n_val, v
        n_val += 1e-4
    check("numerical argmax of eta_2 equals 4", best_n, 4.0, tol=1e-3)
    check("numerical max of eta_2 equals 1/48", best_v, 1.0 / 48.0, tol=1e-8)
    print()
    print("  The SAME value N = 4 is where the specific-heat exponent changes sign:")
    for n_sym, expect in ((3.9, "> 0"), (4.0, "= 0"), (4.1, "< 0")):
        a = alpha_exponent(n_sym, 1.0)
        print(f"    alpha(N = {n_sym}, eps = 1) = {a: .8f}   (expected {expect})")
    print()
    print("  Uniform bound: eta <= eps^2/48 for all N >= 0.")
    worst = max(eta_exponent(n / 10.0, 1.0) for n in range(0, 2001))
    check("max over N in [0, 200] of eta(N, 1)", worst, 1.0 / 48.0, tol=1e-6)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 4: scaling relations, exact and deficient
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_scaling_relations() -> None:
    banner("4.  Scaling relations: which are exact, and the closed-form deficits")
    for n_sym, eps in ((0.0, 1.0), (1.0, 0.5), (3.0, 1.0), (7.5, 0.25), (40.0, 1.0)):
        a = alpha_exponent(n_sym, eps)
        b = beta_op_exponent(n_sym, eps)
        g = gamma_exponent(n_sym, eps)
        nu = nu_exponent(n_sym, eps)
        et = eta_exponent(n_sym, eps)
        de = delta_exponent(eps)
        print(f"  N = {n_sym:<6g} eps = {eps:<5g}")
        check("Rushbrooke  alpha + 2 beta + gamma = 2 (exact)", a + 2 * b + g, 2.0)
        check("gamma = 2 nu (exact)", g, 2.0 * nu)
        check("Fisher deficit  gamma - nu(2-eta) = nu*eta",
              g - nu * (2.0 - et), nu * et)
        check("Josephson deficit  (2-alpha) - (4-eps) nu",
              (2.0 - a) - (4.0 - eps) * nu,
              (n_sym + 2.0) * eps ** 2 / (4.0 * (n_sym + 8.0)))
        check("Widom deficit  1 + gamma/beta - delta",
              1.0 + g / b - de,
              3.0 * eps ** 2 / (n_sym + 8.0 - 3.0 * eps))
        check("coupling identity  3 eta = (2 nu - 1) g*",
              3.0 * et, (2.0 * nu - 1.0) * fixed_point(n_sym, eps))
        check("reciprocality  nu * (1/nu) = 1 - ((N+2)eps/(2(N+8)))^2",
              nu * inv_nu_at_fixed_point(n_sym, eps),
              1.0 - (n_sym + 2.0) ** 2 * eps ** 2 / (4.0 * (n_sym + 8.0) ** 2))
        check("affine invariant  alpha = 2 - 4 nu + eps/2",
              a, 2.0 - 4.0 * nu + eps / 2.0)
        print()
    print("  Note the Widom deficit numerator 3 eps^2 carries no N at all,")
    print("  and every relation that is AFFINE in the exponents is exact.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 5: large N and the spherical model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_large_n() -> None:
    banner("5.  Large N: convergence to the exactly solvable spherical model")
    eps = 1.0
    print("  Spherical model (N = infinity), exact in d = 4 - eps:")
    print("    nu_sph = 1/(d-2) = 1/(2-eps),  alpha_sph = (d-4)/(d-2) = -eps/(2-eps),"
          "  eta_sph = 0")
    print()
    print(f"  {'N':>10s} {'eta_2(N)':>12s} {'nu_1(N)':>12s} {'alpha_1(N)':>12s}")
    for n_sym in (1.0, 10.0, 100.0, 1e3, 1e5, 1e8):
        print(f"  {n_sym:10.0f} {eta_coeff(n_sym):12.3e} {nu_coeff(n_sym):12.8f} "
              f"{alpha_coeff(n_sym):12.8f}")
    print(f"  {'limit':>10s} {0.0:12.3e} {0.25:12.8f} {-0.5:12.8f}")
    print()
    for eps in (0.25, 0.5, 1.0):
        nu_series = 0.5 + eps / 4.0
        nu_exact = 1.0 / (2.0 - eps)
        al_series = -eps / 2.0
        al_exact = -eps / (2.0 - eps)
        check(f"eps={eps}: exact nu-gap = eps^2/(4(2-eps))",
              nu_exact - nu_series, eps ** 2 / (4.0 * (2.0 - eps)))
        print(f"        |gap| = {abs(nu_exact - nu_series):.6f} "
              f"<= eps^2/4 = {eps ** 2 / 4.0:.6f}  "
              f"{'OK' if abs(nu_exact - nu_series) <= eps ** 2 / 4 + TOL else 'FAIL'}")
        check(f"eps={eps}: exact alpha-gap = -eps^2/(2(2-eps))",
              al_exact - al_series, -eps ** 2 / (2.0 * (2.0 - eps)))
        print(f"        |gap| = {abs(al_exact - al_series):.6f} "
              f"<= eps^2/2 = {eps ** 2 / 2.0:.6f}  "
              f"{'OK' if abs(al_exact - al_series) <= eps ** 2 / 2 + TOL else 'FAIL'}")
    print()
    print("  The distinguished value N = -2 (Gaussian locus):")
    check("eta_2(-2) = 0", eta_coeff(-2.0), 0.0)
    check("nu_1(-2)  = 0", nu_coeff(-2.0), 0.0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 6: the discrete infrared flow converges to Wilson-Fisher
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def flow_iterate(n_sym: float, eps: float, step: float, g0: float,
                 n_steps: int) -> List[float]:
    """Discrete infrared Euler flow g_{k+1} = g_k - h beta_N(eps, g_k)."""
    seq: List[float] = [g0]
    g = g0
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        g = g - step * beta_one_loop(n_sym, eps, g)
        seq.append(g)
    return seq


def demo_flow_convergence() -> None:
    banner("6.  The discrete infrared flow: Wilson-Fisher is the attractor")
    eps = 1.0
    print("  g_{k+1} = g_k - h beta_N(eps, g_k),  0 < h <= 1/eps,  g_0 in (0, g*)")
    print("  The basin (0, g*) and the step range are the same for every N >= 0.")
    print()
    for n_sym in (0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 20.0):
        g_star = fixed_point(n_sym, eps)
        for step in (0.25, 1.0):
            g0 = 0.01 * g_star
            seq = flow_iterate(n_sym, eps, step, g0, 4000)
            # non-decreasing overall, and strictly increasing until the
            # sequence saturates at g* to machine precision
            monotone = all(seq[k] <= seq[k + 1] for k in range(len(seq) - 1))
            strict_early = all(seq[k] < seq[k + 1]
                               for k in range(len(seq) - 1)
                               if seq[k] < g_star - 1e-15)
            inside = all(0.0 < x < g_star + TOL for x in seq)
            print(f"  N = {n_sym:<5g} h = {step:<5g}  g* = {g_star:.8f}  "
                  f"limit = {seq[-1]:.8f}  "
                  f"|err| = {abs(seq[-1] - g_star):.2e}  "
                  f"monotone = {monotone}  strictly rising = {strict_early}  "
                  f"in basin = {inside}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 7: two loops, with an N-independent remainder constant
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def bisect_root(f: Callable[[float], float], lo: float, hi: float,
                iters: int = 200) -> float:
    """Bisection for a sign-changing continuous function on [lo, hi]."""
    f_lo = f(lo)
    for _ in range(iters):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        f_mid = f(mid)
        if (f_lo > 0.0) == (f_mid > 0.0):
            lo, f_lo = mid, f_mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)


def demo_two_loop() -> None:
    banner("7.  Two loops: exact root vs prediction, with N-uniform remainder")
    print("  beta_N = -eps g + a g^2 - c g^3,  a = (N+8)/3,  c = (3N+14)/9")
    print("  prediction: g* = 3 eps/(N+8) + 27 c eps^2/(N+8)^3,  error <= eps^3")
    print()
    header = (f"  {'N':>6s} {'eps':>6s} {'one-loop':>12s} {'exact root':>13s}"
              f" {'prediction':>13s} {'|err|':>11s} {'eps^3':>10s} {'12c^2/a^5':>11s}")
    print(header)
    for n_sym in (0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 10.0, 100.0):
        for eps in (0.2, 4.0 / 7.0):
            a = (n_sym + 8.0) / 3.0
            c = two_loop_coeff(n_sym)
            one_loop = eps / a
            pred = one_loop + c * eps ** 2 / a ** 3
            # the non-Gaussian zero solves c r^2 - a r + eps = 0 on [eps/a, 2eps/a]
            root = bisect_root(lambda r: c * r * r - a * r + eps,
                               eps / a, 2.0 * eps / a)
            err = abs(root - pred)
            residual = beta_two_loop(n_sym, c, eps, root)
            assert abs(residual) < 1e-10, residual
            assert root >= one_loop - TOL
            assert err <= eps ** 3 + TOL
            print(f"  {n_sym:6.0f} {eps:6.3f} {one_loop:12.8f} {root:13.9f}"
                  f" {pred:13.9f} {err:11.3e} {eps ** 3:10.3e}"
                  f" {12 * c ** 2 / a ** 5:11.4f}")
    print()
    print("  The last column is the a-priori remainder constant 12 c^2 / a^5.")
    print("  It stays below 1 for every N >= 0 because a = (N+8)/3 enters to the")
    print("  fifth power while c grows only linearly: the two-loop remainder is")
    print("  uniform BECAUSE the fixed-point coupling shrinks like 1/N.")
    print()
    print("  Two-loop correction always pushes the coupling up:")
    for n_sym in (0.0, 2.0, 9.0):
        one = fixed_point(n_sym, 0.5)
        two = one + 27.0 * two_loop_coeff(n_sym) * 0.25 / (n_sym + 8.0) ** 3
        print(f"    N = {n_sym:<4g}  one-loop {one:.8f}  <  two-loop {two:.8f}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 8: the master table at eps = 1
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_table() -> None:
    banner("8.  The exponent table at eps = 1 (three dimensions)")
    print(f"  {'N':>8s} {'g*':>9s} {'eta':>9s} {'nu':>9s} {'gamma':>9s}"
          f" {'alpha':>9s} {'beta':>9s} {'delta':>7s} {'omega':>7s}")
    rows: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 10.0, 1e9)
    for n_sym in rows:
        e = all_exponents(n_sym, 1.0)
        label = "inf" if n_sym > 1e8 else f"{n_sym:.0f}"
        print(f"  {label:>8s} {e['g*']:9.4f} {e['eta']:9.5f} {e['nu']:9.4f}"
              f" {e['gamma']:9.4f} {e['alpha']:9.4f} {e['beta']:9.4f}"
              f" {e['delta']:7.2f} {e['omega']:7.2f}")
    print()
    print("  Reference three-dimensional estimates for comparison:")
    print("    Ising     (N=1):  nu ~ 0.630, gamma ~ 1.237, eta ~ 0.036")
    print("    XY        (N=2):  nu ~ 0.672, gamma ~ 1.318, eta ~ 0.038")
    print("    Heisenberg(N=3):  nu ~ 0.711, gamma ~ 1.396, eta ~ 0.037")
    print("  A first-order truncation evaluated at eps = 1 captures the correct")
    print("  ordering and the correct direction of departure from mean field.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    print("Critical exponents of the O(N) model, uniformly in N")
    print("One-loop beta function: beta_N(eps, g) = -eps g + ((N+8)/3) g^2")
    demo_fixed_points()
    demo_omega_universality()
    demo_extremum_at_four()
    demo_scaling_relations()
    demo_large_n()
    demo_flow_convergence()
    demo_two_loop()
    demo_table()
    banner("All numerical checks completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Comprehensive Verification Suite for the O(N) Critical Exponents
demos.description: A single self-contained script that reconstructs the entire development numerically and checks every claim to machine precision. It classifies the fixed points of the one-loop beta function and confirms that the Gaussian slope is -eps while the Wilson-Fisher slope is exactly +eps for every N; verifies by finite differences that the correction-to-scaling exponent omega equals eps independently of the symmetry index; locates the maximum of the anomalous-dimension coefficient numerically and confirms it sits at N = 4 with value 1/48; evaluates all four classical scaling relations across a range of (N, eps) and matches each deficit against its closed form, showing that Rushbrooke's relation is an exact identity while Fisher's, Josephson's and Widom's carry computable O(eps^2) defects; compares the large-N limits with the exactly solvable spherical model and confirms the explicit eps^2/4 and eps^2/2 error bounds; iterates the discrete infrared flow from inside the basin (0, g*) and confirms monotone convergence to the Wilson-Fisher coupling for several N and step sizes; and solves the two-loop cubic by bisection, checking that the exact root always lies within the certified eps^3 envelope of the predicted expansion. Requires only the Python standard library.
demos.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Numerical demonstrations for the critical exponents of the O(N) model,
uniformly in the symmetry index N.

Everything in this file is derived from a single one-loop beta function

    beta_N(eps, g) = -eps * g + ((N + 8) / 3) * g**2,

whose only zeros are the Gaussian coupling g = 0 and the Wilson-Fisher
coupling g* = 3*eps/(N + 8).  Substituting g* into the standard scaling
functions produces the first terms of the critical exponents as explicit
rational functions of N:

    eta   = (N+2) eps^2 / (2 (N+8)^2)
    nu    = 1/2 + (N+2) eps / (4 (N+8))
    gamma = 1 + (N+2) eps / (2 (N+8))
    alpha = (4-N) eps / (2 (N+8))
    beta  = 1/2 - 3 eps / (2 (N+8))
    delta = 3 + eps
    omega = eps

The script verifies, numerically and to machine precision:

  1. the fixed-point classification and the value of g*;
  2. reduction to the classical one-component (Ising) values at N = 1;
  3. omega = d(beta_N)/dg at g*, equal to eps for every N;
  4. maximality of the eta coefficient exactly at N = 4, value 1/48;
  5. the sign flip of the specific-heat exponent exactly at N = 4;
  6. Rushbrooke's relation as an exact identity in (N, eps);
  7. the closed-form deficits of Fisher, Josephson and Widom;
  8. the coupling-exponent identity 3 eta = (2 nu - 1) g*;
  9. large-N limits and agreement with the exactly solvable spherical model;
 10. convergence of the discrete infrared flow to g*, N-uniformly;
 11. two-loop existence with an N-independent O(eps^3) remainder constant.

Requires only the Python standard library.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

TOL: float = 1e-12


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The one-loop flow
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def beta_one_loop(n_sym: float, eps: float, g: float) -> float:
    """One-loop beta function -eps*g + ((N+8)/3) g^2."""
    return -eps * g + ((n_sym + 8.0) / 3.0) * g * g


def beta_derivative(n_sym: float, eps: float, g: float) -> float:
    """Exact derivative d(beta)/dg = -eps + 2 ((N+8)/3) g."""
    return -eps + 2.0 * ((n_sym + 8.0) / 3.0) * g


def fixed_point(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Wilson-Fisher coupling g* = 3 eps / (N + 8)."""
    return 3.0 * eps / (n_sym + 8.0)


def beta_two_loop(n_sym: float, c_two: float, eps: float, g: float) -> float:
    """Two-loop beta function -eps*g + ((N+8)/3) g^2 - c g^3."""
    return beta_one_loop(n_sym, eps, g) - c_two * g ** 3


def two_loop_coeff(n_sym: float) -> float:
    """Standard two-loop coefficient c(N) = (3N + 14)/9 in this normalisation."""
    return (3.0 * n_sym + 14.0) / 9.0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The critical exponents
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def eta_exponent(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Anomalous dimension eta = (N+2) eps^2 / (2 (N+8)^2)."""
    return (n_sym + 2.0) * eps ** 2 / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0) ** 2)


def nu_exponent(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Correlation-length exponent nu = 1/2 + (N+2) eps / (4 (N+8))."""
    return 0.5 + (n_sym + 2.0) * eps / (4.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


def inv_nu_at_fixed_point(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """1/nu evaluated at the fixed point: 2 - (N+2) eps / (N+8)."""
    return 2.0 - (n_sym + 2.0) * eps / (n_sym + 8.0)


def gamma_exponent(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Susceptibility exponent gamma = 1 + (N+2) eps / (2 (N+8))."""
    return 1.0 + (n_sym + 2.0) * eps / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


def alpha_exponent(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Specific-heat exponent alpha = (4-N) eps / (2 (N+8))."""
    return (4.0 - n_sym) * eps / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


def beta_op_exponent(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> float:
    """Order-parameter exponent beta = 1/2 - 3 eps / (2 (N+8))."""
    return 0.5 - 3.0 * eps / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


def delta_exponent(eps: float) -> float:
    """Critical-isotherm exponent delta = 3 + eps (independent of N)."""
    return 3.0 + eps


def omega_exponent(eps: float) -> float:
    """Correction-to-scaling exponent omega = eps (independent of N)."""
    return eps


def all_exponents(n_sym: float, eps: float) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """Return the full exponent dictionary at given (N, eps)."""
    return {
        "g*": fixed_point(n_sym, eps),
        "eta": eta_exponent(n_sym, eps),
        "nu": nu_exponent(n_sym, eps),
        "gamma": gamma_exponent(n_sym, eps),
        "alpha": alpha_exponent(n_sym, eps),
        "beta": beta_op_exponent(n_sym, eps),
        "delta": delta_exponent(eps),
        "omega": omega_exponent(eps),
    }


# Leading coefficients as functions of N alone.


def eta_coeff(n_sym: float) -> float:
    """eta_2(N) = (N+2) / (2 (N+8)^2), the coefficient of eps^2 in eta."""
    return (n_sym + 2.0) / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0) ** 2)


def nu_coeff(n_sym: float) -> float:
    """nu_1(N) = (N+2) / (4 (N+8)), the coefficient of eps in nu."""
    return (n_sym + 2.0) / (4.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


def alpha_coeff(n_sym: float) -> float:
    """alpha_1(N) = (4-N) / (2 (N+8)), the coefficient of eps in alpha."""
    return (4.0 - n_sym) / (2.0 * (n_sym + 8.0))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Reporting helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def check(label: str, lhs: float, rhs: float, tol: float = TOL) -> bool:
    """Print and return the outcome of a numerical equality assertion."""
    ok = abs(lhs - rhs) <= tol * max(1.0, abs(lhs), abs(rhs))
    mark = "OK " if ok else "FAIL"
    print(f"  [{mark}] {label:<52s} {lhs: .12f}  vs {rhs: .12f}")
    return ok


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 1: fixed-point classification and reduction at N = 1
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_fixed_points() -> None:
    banner("1.  Fixed points of the one-loop flow, and the Ising slice")
    eps = 1.0
    print("  beta_N(eps, g) = -eps g + ((N+8)/3) g^2 ;  eps = 1")
    print()
    print(f"  {'N':>6s} {'g*':>12s} {'beta(g*)':>14s} {'beta(0)':>10s}"
          f" {'slope at 0':>12s} {'slope at g*':>12s}")
    for n_sym in (0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 10.0, 100.0):
        g_star = fixed_point(n_sym, eps)
        print(f"  {n_sym:6.0f} {g_star:12.8f} {beta_one_loop(n_sym, eps, g_star):14.2e}"
              f" {beta_one_loop(n_sym, eps, 0.0):10.2e}"
              f" {beta_derivative(n_sym, eps, 0.0):12.6f}"
              f" {beta_derivative(n_sym, eps, g_star):12.6f}")
    print()
    print("  The Gaussian point has slope -eps < 0 (infrared-repulsive);")
    print("  the Wilson-Fisher point has slope exactly +eps > 0 for EVERY N.")
    print()
    print("  Reduction to the one-component (Ising) theory at N = 1, eps = 1:")
    check("g*(1, 1) = 1/3", fixed_point(1.0, 1.0), 1.0 / 3.0)
    check("eta(1, 1) = 1/54", eta_exponent(1.0, 1.0), 1.0 / 54.0)
    check("nu(1, 1) = 1/2 + 1/12", nu_exponent(1.0, 1.0), 0.5 + 1.0 / 12.0)
    check("gamma(1, 1) = 1 + 1/6", gamma_exponent(1.0, 1.0), 1.0 + 1.0 / 6.0)
    check("alpha(1, 1) = 1/6", alpha_exponent(1.0, 1.0), 1.0 / 6.0)
    check("beta(1, 1) = 1/2 - 1/6", beta_op_exponent(1.0, 1.0), 0.5 - 1.0 / 6.0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 2: omega is the slope, universally
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def numerical_derivative(f: Callable[[float], float], x: float,
                         h: float = 1e-6) -> float:
    """Central finite difference."""
    return (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2.0 * h)


def demo_omega_universality() -> None:
    banner("2.  omega = d(beta)/dg at the fixed point equals eps for every N")
    for eps in (0.25, 0.5, 1.0):
        print(f"  eps = {eps}")
        for n_sym in (0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 7.0, 50.0):
            g_star = fixed_point(n_sym, eps)
            num = numerical_derivative(lambda g: beta_one_loop(n_sym, eps, g), g_star)
            check(f"N = {n_sym:<5g}  finite-difference slope = eps",
                  num, omega_exponent(eps), tol=1e-6)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 3: the extremum at N = 4
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_extremum_at_four() -> None:
    banner("3.  The anomalous-dimension coefficient peaks exactly at N = 4")
    print("  eta_2(N) = (N+2) / (2 (N+8)^2);   claim: max = 1/48 at N = 4")
    print()
    print(f"  {'N':>8s} {'eta_2(N)':>14s} {'1/48 - eta_2':>16s} "
          f"{'alpha_1(N)':>12s}")
    grid: List[float] = [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0, 8.0, 20.0, 200.0]
    for n_sym in grid:
        print(f"  {n_sym:8.2f} {eta_coeff(n_sym):14.10f} "
              f"{1.0 / 48.0 - eta_coeff(n_sym):16.3e} {alpha_coeff(n_sym):12.6f}")
    print()
    # Fine scan to locate the maximiser numerically.
    best_n, best_v = -8.0, -math.inf
    n_val = 0.0
    while n_val <= 12.0:
        v = eta_coeff(n_val)
        if v > best_v:
            best_n, best_v = n_val, v
        n_val += 1e-4
    check("numerical argmax of eta_2 equals 4", best_n, 4.0, tol=1e-3)
    check("numerical max of eta_2 equals 1/48", best_v, 1.0 / 48.0, tol=1e-8)
    print()
    print("  The SAME value N = 4 is where the specific-heat exponent changes sign:")
    for n_sym, expect in ((3.9, "> 0"), (4.0, "= 0"), (4.1, "< 0")):
        a = alpha_exponent(n_sym, 1.0)
        print(f"    alpha(N = {n_sym}, eps = 1) = {a: .8f}   (expected {expect})")
    print()
    print("  Uniform bound: eta <= eps^2/48 for all N >= 0.")
    worst = max(eta_exponent(n / 10.0, 1.0) for n in range(0, 2001))
    check("max over N in [0, 200] of eta(N, 1)", worst, 1.0 / 48.0, tol=1e-6)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 4: scaling relations, exact and deficient
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_scaling_relations() -> None:
    banner("4.  Scaling relations: which are exact, and the closed-form deficits")
    for n_sym, eps in ((0.0, 1.0), (1.0, 0.5), (3.0, 1.0), (7.5, 0.25), (40.0, 1.0)):
        a = alpha_exponent(n_sym, eps)
        b = beta_op_exponent(n_sym, eps)
        g = gamma_exponent(n_sym, eps)
        nu = nu_exponent(n_sym, eps)
        et = eta_exponent(n_sym, eps)
        de = delta_exponent(eps)
        print(f"  N = {n_sym:<6g} eps = {eps:<5g}")
        check("Rushbrooke  alpha + 2 beta + gamma = 2 (exact)", a + 2 * b + g, 2.0)
        check("gamma = 2 nu (exact)", g, 2.0 * nu)
        check("Fisher deficit  gamma - nu(2-eta) = nu*eta",
              g - nu * (2.0 - et), nu * et)
        check("Josephson deficit  (2-alpha) - (4-eps) nu",
              (2.0 - a) - (4.0 - eps) * nu,
              (n_sym + 2.0) * eps ** 2 / (4.0 * (n_sym + 8.0)))
        check("Widom deficit  1 + gamma/beta - delta",
              1.0 + g / b - de,
              3.0 * eps ** 2 / (n_sym + 8.0 - 3.0 * eps))
        check("coupling identity  3 eta = (2 nu - 1) g*",
              3.0 * et, (2.0 * nu - 1.0) * fixed_point(n_sym, eps))
        check("reciprocality  nu * (1/nu) = 1 - ((N+2)eps/(2(N+8)))^2",
              nu * inv_nu_at_fixed_point(n_sym, eps),
              1.0 - (n_sym + 2.0) ** 2 * eps ** 2 / (4.0 * (n_sym + 8.0) ** 2))
        check("affine invariant  alpha = 2 - 4 nu + eps/2",
              a, 2.0 - 4.0 * nu + eps / 2.0)
        print()
    print("  Note the Widom deficit numerator 3 eps^2 carries no N at all,")
    print("  and every relation that is AFFINE in the exponents is exact.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 5: large N and the spherical model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_large_n() -> None:
    banner("5.  Large N: convergence to the exactly solvable spherical model")
    eps = 1.0
    print("  Spherical model (N = infinity), exact in d = 4 - eps:")
    print("    nu_sph = 1/(d-2) = 1/(2-eps),  alpha_sph = (d-4)/(d-2) = -eps/(2-eps),"
          "  eta_sph = 0")
    print()
    print(f"  {'N':>10s} {'eta_2(N)':>12s} {'nu_1(N)':>12s} {'alpha_1(N)':>12s}")
    for n_sym in (1.0, 10.0, 100.0, 1e3, 1e5, 1e8):
        print(f"  {n_sym:10.0f} {eta_coeff(n_sym):12.3e} {nu_coeff(n_sym):12.8f} "
              f"{alpha_coeff(n_sym):12.8f}")
    print(f"  {'limit':>10s} {0.0:12.3e} {0.25:12.8f} {-0.5:12.8f}")
    print()
    for eps in (0.25, 0.5, 1.0):
        nu_series = 0.5 + eps / 4.0
        nu_exact = 1.0 / (2.0 - eps)
        al_series = -eps / 2.0
        al_exact = -eps / (2.0 - eps)
        check(f"eps={eps}: exact nu-gap = eps^2/(4(2-eps))",
              nu_exact - nu_series, eps ** 2 / (4.0 * (2.0 - eps)))
        print(f"        |gap| = {abs(nu_exact - nu_series):.6f} "
              f"<= eps^2/4 = {eps ** 2 / 4.0:.6f}  "
              f"{'OK' if abs(nu_exact - nu_series) <= eps ** 2 / 4 + TOL else 'FAIL'}")
        check(f"eps={eps}: exact alpha-gap = -eps^2/(2(2-eps))",
              al_exact - al_series, -eps ** 2 / (2.0 * (2.0 - eps)))
        print(f"        |gap| = {abs(al_exact - al_series):.6f} "
              f"<= eps^2/2 = {eps ** 2 / 2.0:.6f}  "
              f"{'OK' if abs(al_exact - al_series) <= eps ** 2 / 2 + TOL else 'FAIL'}")
    print()
    print("  The distinguished value N = -2 (Gaussian locus):")
    check("eta_2(-2) = 0", eta_coeff(-2.0), 0.0)
    check("nu_1(-2)  = 0", nu_coeff(-2.0), 0.0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 6: the discrete infrared flow converges to Wilson-Fisher
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def flow_iterate(n_sym: float, eps: float, step: float, g0: float,
                 n_steps: int) -> List[float]:
    """Discrete infrared Euler flow g_{k+1} = g_k - h beta_N(eps, g_k)."""
    seq: List[float] = [g0]
    g = g0
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        g = g - step * beta_one_loop(n_sym, eps, g)
        seq.append(g)
    return seq


def demo_flow_convergence() -> None:
    banner("6.  The discrete infrared flow: Wilson-Fisher is the attractor")
    eps = 1.0
    print("  g_{k+1} = g_k - h beta_N(eps, g_k),  0 < h <= 1/eps,  g_0 in (0, g*)")
    print("  The basin (0, g*) and the step range are the same for every N >= 0.")
    print()
    for n_sym in (0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 20.0):
        g_star = fixed_point(n_sym, eps)
        for step in (0.25, 1.0):
            g0 = 0.01 * g_star
            seq = flow_iterate(n_sym, eps, step, g0, 4000)
            # non-decreasing overall, and strictly increasing until the
            # sequence saturates at g* to machine precision
            monotone = all(seq[k] <= seq[k + 1] for k in range(len(seq) - 1))
            strict_early = all(seq[k] < seq[k + 1]
                               for k in range(len(seq) - 1)
                               if seq[k] < g_star - 1e-15)
            inside = all(0.0 < x < g_star + TOL for x in seq)
            print(f"  N = {n_sym:<5g} h = {step:<5g}  g* = {g_star:.8f}  "
                  f"limit = {seq[-1]:.8f}  "
                  f"|err| = {abs(seq[-1] - g_star):.2e}  "
                  f"monotone = {monotone}  strictly rising = {strict_early}  "
                  f"in basin = {inside}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 7: two loops, with an N-independent remainder constant
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def bisect_root(f: Callable[[float], float], lo: float, hi: float,
                iters: int = 200) -> float:
    """Bisection for a sign-changing continuous function on [lo, hi]."""
    f_lo = f(lo)
    for _ in range(iters):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        f_mid = f(mid)
        if (f_lo > 0.0) == (f_mid > 0.0):
            lo, f_lo = mid, f_mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return 0.5 * (lo + hi)


def demo_two_loop() -> None:
    banner("7.  Two loops: exact root vs prediction, with N-uniform remainder")
    print("  beta_N = -eps g + a g^2 - c g^3,  a = (N+8)/3,  c = (3N+14)/9")
    print("  prediction: g* = 3 eps/(N+8) + 27 c eps^2/(N+8)^3,  error <= eps^3")
    print()
    header = (f"  {'N':>6s} {'eps':>6s} {'one-loop':>12s} {'exact root':>13s}"
              f" {'prediction':>13s} {'|err|':>11s} {'eps^3':>10s} {'12c^2/a^5':>11s}")
    print(header)
    for n_sym in (0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 10.0, 100.0):
        for eps in (0.2, 4.0 / 7.0):
            a = (n_sym + 8.0) / 3.0
            c = two_loop_coeff(n_sym)
            one_loop = eps / a
            pred = one_loop + c * eps ** 2 / a ** 3
            # the non-Gaussian zero solves c r^2 - a r + eps = 0 on [eps/a, 2eps/a]
            root = bisect_root(lambda r: c * r * r - a * r + eps,
                               eps / a, 2.0 * eps / a)
            err = abs(root - pred)
            residual = beta_two_loop(n_sym, c, eps, root)
            assert abs(residual) < 1e-10, residual
            assert root >= one_loop - TOL
            assert err <= eps ** 3 + TOL
            print(f"  {n_sym:6.0f} {eps:6.3f} {one_loop:12.8f} {root:13.9f}"
                  f" {pred:13.9f} {err:11.3e} {eps ** 3:10.3e}"
                  f" {12 * c ** 2 / a ** 5:11.4f}")
    print()
    print("  The last column is the a-priori remainder constant 12 c^2 / a^5.")
    print("  It stays below 1 for every N >= 0 because a = (N+8)/3 enters to the")
    print("  fifth power while c grows only linearly: the two-loop remainder is")
    print("  uniform BECAUSE the fixed-point coupling shrinks like 1/N.")
    print()
    print("  Two-loop correction always pushes the coupling up:")
    for n_sym in (0.0, 2.0, 9.0):
        one = fixed_point(n_sym, 0.5)
        two = one + 27.0 * two_loop_coeff(n_sym) * 0.25 / (n_sym + 8.0) ** 3
        print(f"    N = {n_sym:<4g}  one-loop {one:.8f}  <  two-loop {two:.8f}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo 8: the master table at eps = 1
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_table() -> None:
    banner("8.  The exponent table at eps = 1 (three dimensions)")
    print(f"  {'N':>8s} {'g*':>9s} {'eta':>9s} {'nu':>9s} {'gamma':>9s}"
          f" {'alpha':>9s} {'beta':>9s} {'delta':>7s} {'omega':>7s}")
    rows: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 10.0, 1e9)
    for n_sym in rows:
        e = all_exponents(n_sym, 1.0)
        label = "inf" if n_sym > 1e8 else f"{n_sym:.0f}"
        print(f"  {label:>8s} {e['g*']:9.4f} {e['eta']:9.5f} {e['nu']:9.4f}"
              f" {e['gamma']:9.4f} {e['alpha']:9.4f} {e['beta']:9.4f}"
              f" {e['delta']:7.2f} {e['omega']:7.2f}")
    print()
    print("  Reference three-dimensional estimates for comparison:")
    print("    Ising     (N=1):  nu ~ 0.630, gamma ~ 1.237, eta ~ 0.036")
    print("    XY        (N=2):  nu ~ 0.672, gamma ~ 1.318, eta ~ 0.038")
    print("    Heisenberg(N=3):  nu ~ 0.711, gamma ~ 1.396, eta ~ 0.037")
    print("  A first-order truncation evaluated at eps = 1 captures the correct")
    print("  ordering and the correct direction of departure from mean field.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    print("Critical exponents of the O(N) model, uniformly in N")
    print("One-loop beta function: beta_N(eps, g) = -eps g + ((N+8)/3) g^2")
    demo_fixed_points()
    demo_omega_universality()
    demo_extremum_at_four()
    demo_scaling_relations()
    demo_large_n()
    demo_flow_convergence()
    demo_two_loop()
    demo_table()
    banner("All numerical checks completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Wilson-Fisher Exponent Evaluation from the One-Loop Beta Function
algorithms.description: Given a symmetry index N and a dimensional deficit eps with d = 4 - eps, this routine locates the non-Gaussian zero of the one-loop beta function by exact factorisation rather than numerically: the polynomial -eps g + ((N+8)/3) g^2 factors as g times a linear term, so the only zeros are 0 and 3 eps/(N+8), and the excluded point N = -8 is detected and reported. The fixed-point coupling is then substituted into the scaling functions eta(N, g) = ((N+2)/18) g^2 and 1/nu(N, g) = 2 - ((N+2)/3) g to produce the complete first-order exponent vector. A companion routine evaluates all four classical scaling relations and compares each measured deficit against its closed form, making visible the fact that Rushbrooke's relation is exact while the three nonlinear relations are not. Complexity: O(1) arithmetic operations per (N, eps) pair, hence O(M) for a table over M values of N; there is no iteration and no numerical root-finding anywhere, so the output is exact up to floating-point rounding.
algorithms.pseudocode:
function WILSON_FISHER_COUPLING(N, eps):
    if N + 8 = 0 then
        raise 'excluded point: fixed point diverges'
    return 3 * eps / (N + 8)          # exact factorisation of the quadratic

function EXPONENT_VECTOR(N, eps):
    D    <- N + 8
    gs   <- WILSON_FISHER_COUPLING(N, eps)
    eta  <- ((N + 2) / 18) * gs^2     # two-loop anomalous dimension at g*
    invnu<- 2 - ((N + 2) / 3) * gs    # one-loop 1/nu at g*
    nu   <- 1/2 + (N + 2) * eps / (4 * D)
    gamma<- 1   + (N + 2) * eps / (2 * D)
    alpha<- (4 - N) * eps / (2 * D)
